pages.x: When Japan surrendered in 1945, two young American officers, working with a magazine map, chose the 38th parallel to divide Korea: Soviet troops would take the surrender north of it, Americans south of it. The line hardened into two states, the communist North under Kim Il Sung and the South under Syngman Rhee.

With Stalin's blessing, Kim Il Sung sent his Soviet-armed army across the line on 25 June 1950. Seoul fell in three days, and the South's forces and their few American allies were pushed back into a small corner around the port of Busan.

The United Nations sent an army led by the United States, with soldiers from 16 countries. In September General Douglas MacArthur landed behind the North Korean lines at Inchon, in a daring attack from the sea, and took back Seoul. UN forces then drove north almost to the Chinese border.

In late October hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers crossed the Yalu River in secret. They struck in the freezing mountains and drove the UN forces back south of Seoul. When MacArthur called for bombing China, even with atomic bombs, President Truman fired him.

From 1951 the war bogged down into trench fighting near the 38th parallel, much like the First World War, while peace talks dragged on for two years, mainly over prisoners who did not want to go home. American bombing flattened almost every town in the North.

pages.x: An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. The new border, close to the old line, became the most heavily guarded in the world, with a demilitarised zone four kilometres wide between the two Koreas. No peace treaty has ever been signed.

Korea is still divided. The South grew into one of the world's richest democracies, while the North became a closed dictatorship ruled by Kim's son and grandson, with nuclear weapons. Millions of families were split by the war, and few have ever seen their relatives across the line again.
